Clinical Neuroscience Lecture: Mending the Mind: From Single Neurons to Memory Neuroprosthetics — Itzhak Fried
description:
Neurosurgical opportunities to record and stimulate single neurons in humans who can report their memories and intentions provide a unique window into the biology of mind. The speaker will present neuronal codes for space, time, and conceptual content derived from single-neuron and population activity in the hippocampal-entorhinal system; review modulation across wake-sleep cycles to enhance memory encoding and consolidation; and discuss ongoing work on targeted modification of specific memories.

To submit a question during the session, use the annual meeting mobile app.

Glial Regulation of Motor Circuit Formation, Function, and Regeneration — Sarah Ackerman
description: From simple planaria to humans, proper assembly and maintenance of motor circuits is key to organismal survival. Recent data indicate that glia, a heterogeneous group of non-neuronal cells within the nervous system, directly communicate with neurons to tune motor circuit dynamics. This minisymposium will highlight recent advances in our understanding of how diverse glial cell types promote proper formation, function, and reconstruction of the key circuits that drive motor behavior.
objectives: Answer long-standing questions: does motor circuit regeneration mimic development?
Identify conserved principles of motor circuit structure/function across species.
Spark new questions related to glia-glia signaling in motor circuits.

title: Presidential Special Lecture: Rett Syndrome and MeCP2 Disorders: Genes, Circuits, and Treatment Strategies — Huda Y. Zoghbi
description: Rett syndrome is a severe childhood neurological disorder caused by mutations in methyl CpG binding protein 2 (MeCP2). The brain is acutely sensitive to MeCP2 levels — both loss and gain of function produce neurological disease in mice and humans. This lecture will cover cell-specific molecular changes downstream of MeCP2 dysfunction, the neuronal and circuit abnormalities driving Rett phenotypes, and therapeutic strategies targeting MeCP2 loss and gain.

Amygdala-Centered Cortico-Subcortical Networks in Social Perception and Decision-Making — Sai Sun
description: This symposium advances causal understanding of amygdala-centered subcortical networks underlying social perception, affective processing, and motivational decision-making. Integrating intracranial recordings, neurosurgical and neuromodulatory approaches, and computational modeling, it highlights how frontal-striatal-amygdala circuits shape emotional behavior in healthy and clinical populations.
objectives: Describe how amygdala-centered cortico–subcortical networks contribute to social perception and affective decision-making across healthy and clinical populations.
Compare invasive, noninvasive, and minimally invasive methods for causally probing and modulating amygdala-centered circuits, including stimulation, ablation, and neuromodulation approaches.
Evaluate how circuit-level and computational models of amygdala-centered networks inform mechanisms of emotional bias and guide translational interventions in neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: From Pathways to Pathology: High-Plex Spatial Proteomics From 2D Single-Cell to 3D Neuroscience — Miranda Orr
description: Single-cell studies have revealed selective alterations in brain cell types during development, aging and neurodegenerative disease, but most rely on dissociated tissue and transcriptomics, losing spatial context and protein-level biology. This minisymposium highlights spatial proteomic imaging, from high-plex single-cell mapping to 3D spatial proteomics, to localize pathways in intact brain tissue and define cell- and circuit-level mechanisms.
objectives: Describe major spatial proteomic imaging modalities (high-plex to 3D) and the types of biological questions each is best suited to address in brain aging and neurodegeneration.
Interpret spatial proteomic patterns at the cellular and microenvironment level (e.g., neuron–glia niches, pathology-associated states) to infer pathway activation and disease-relevant mechanisms.
Evaluate strategies for integrating spatial proteomics with other spatial modalities and neuropathology to increase mechanistic interpretability and translational relevance.

Molecular Mechanisms Governing Cerebral Cortex Formation and Their Disruption in Human Developmental Disorders — Linda Richards
description: The development of the earliest stages of cerebral cortex formation is critical for establishing the correct number and types of neurons, and precise areas and circuits devoted to processing different types of information. Recent advances in the transcriptional pathways regulating these early processes will be addressed, highlighting how these mechanisms allow a deeper understanding of the etiology of congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders of the human cerebral cortex.
objectives: Understand the molecular mechanisms governing early cortical development.
Identify key genes implicated in human cortical developmental disorders.
Describe how specific genes disrupt early cellular populations and lead to downstream effects on brain formation.

Novel Synaptic Mechanisms Underlying Antidepressant-Like Behaviors — Zhenzhong Ma
description: Novel antidepressants, such as ketamine and psilocybin, produce rapid and sustained therapeutic effects in patients with depression. Neuroplasticity, characterized by adaptive changes in synaptic strength, spinogenesis, and circuit plasticity across multiple brain regions, is essential for antidepressant and stress responses. This minisymposium highlights recent advances in elucidating these critical synaptic mechanisms, which may inform the development of improved antidepressant therapies.
objectives: Enhance understanding of the synaptic and circuit mechanisms behind ketamine and psychedelics' antidepressant effects. Help broaden knowledge of neuroplasticity and its critical role in regulating antidepressant and stress responses.

Learn novel approaches for analyzing these mechanisms, including but not limited to electrophysiology, advanced imaging, and optical/pharmacological neuromodulation. This will offer a valuable overview of the experimental tools used in the field.

Help answer critical questions, such as: Can we manipulate antidepressant-induced synaptic plasticity? How can we leverage these mechanisms to improve drug effects? Can we identify new drug targets to develop better antidepressant treatments?

title: Cerebrospinal Fluid: Form, Flow, and Function — Laura Lewis
description: Recent work has ushered in a new era for the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), revealing many opportunities for investigating, diagnosing, and potentially treating brain disorders. However, CSF production, circulation, and functions represent some of the least understood areas in neuroscience. This session will bring together an interdisciplinary group of scientists to share recent discoveries and conceptual advancements in this emerging field.
objectives: Discuss questions and challenges of CSF research.
Identify neural mechanisms that regulate neurovascular and CSF dynamics including during sleep.
Understand how CSF clearance from the brain is linked to brain immune surveillance.

title: From Bed to Bench and Back Again: Integrating Patient Insight Into Translational Neuroscience — Kirk Leech
description: This roundtable explores how patient perspectives can actively shape translational neuroscience. Drawing on EARA’s Patient Discovery Project and in partnership with patient advocacy groups, the session highlights how structured patient–clinician-researcher dialogue can demonstrate real-world impact of neuroscience research, while supporting sustainable, patient-centered innovation.
objectives: Understand how patient-derived insights can inform preclinical study design and improve translational relevance.
Evaluate the role of animal research that is transparent and responsive to patient needs in developing safe and effective neurotherapies.
Identify practical ways to foster dialogue between patients, basic science researchers, and clinical researchers in neuroscience.

The Era of Neuroscience Innovation: How Federal Investment Seeds Innovation Leading to Cures and Treatments
description: New cures and treatments depend on sustained investment in NIH-funded research. This congressional briefing, co-hosted by the American Brain Coalition in cooperation with the Congressional Neuroscience Caucus, will explore how neuroscientists are harnessing gene therapy to treat neurological developmental disorders. Panelists will discuss groundbreaking advancements, the scientific discoveries that made them possible, and what the future holds for the next generation of gene therapies.
